judgments.title: LEE KUAH SHYAN v Lee Kuah Woon & ors
judgments.catchwords: Originating Summons for declaratory relief as to the true construction of the Last Will and Testament - testator’s intention as expressed in the words of the will read as a whole, and not his unexpressed subjective wishes - Second, the court will, so far as the language permits, prefer a construction that gives every clause some operative effect over one that renders any clause meaningless - where two constructions are reasonably open, and one produces an intestacy, be it whole or partial, while the other avoids it, the court prefers the construction that avoids intestacy - the court is not entitled to make a fresh will for the testator merely because it suspects that he did not mean what he plainly said - the court may inform itself of the testator’s actual circumstances at the time he made the will, this includes his family, his property, and his business relationships, to understand what he meant by the words he used, before concluding that those words are ambiguous or deciding how any ambiguity is to be resolved. - company is a legal person distinct from its members, and that a shareholder, even one holding practically the whole of the issued capital, has no legal or equitable proprietary interest in the company’s assets.

judgments.title: TERNARY TAX ADVISORS SDN BHD v JES TAX CONSULTANTS SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: 1. There is perhaps some irony in this dispute. The Plaintiff and the Defendant are companies engaged in tax consultancy. They were established and are run by individuals who are themselves tax practitioners. In their professional work, the parties are accustomed to dealing with figures, reconciling accounts and ensuring accuracy in financial matters. Yet, in this case, their respective accounts of contributions, payments and expenses are far from reconcilable. Each party relies on its own invoices, payment records and calculations, while disputing those produced by the other. This Court has therefore had to examine an extensive body of documentary evidence and consider the testimony of the witnesses over the course of the trial. At the heart of the dispute lies a straightforward question. Did the parties honour the obligations they had undertaken under the Trust Deed? 10. Accordingly, while the Plaintiffs broad categorisation provides a convenient framework, the Court considers that the real controversy between the parties may be distilled into the following questions: First, what were the respective rights and obligations of the parties under the Trust Deed and did either party breach those obligations, including by the Plaintiffs locking of the premises; Second, did the Letter of Offer and the subsequent dealings between the parties result in a binding agreement for the sale of the Plaintiffs one-half share or did the parties' negotiations fail to culminate in a concluded agreement; Third, what were the parties' respective rights to possession and rental during the relevant periods; Fourth, what sums were properly payable by either party in respect of the various outgoings and payments and was any set-off available; and Finally, what relief, if any, should follow from the Court's findings on those matters. 11. It is against that framework that the evidence and the parties respective contentions will be considered.

judgments.title: XXXX & ors v Dr Sumayyah binti Mohd Faridz & ors

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: Dr Nur Zawani binti Mohd Zain

judgments.catchwords: 1. This action arises from injuries sustained by the 1st Plaintiff during her birth at Hospital Melaka on 18 February 2018. The claim is founded upon allegations of medical negligence in the management of labour and delivery which resulted in severe and permanent neurological injury to the 1st Plaintiff. 2. Following the close of the Plaintiffs’ case, the 11th Defendant (D11) admitted liability. Accordingly, the sole issue remaining for determination is the assessment of damages consequent upon the injuries sustained by the 1st Plaintiff. 3. The evidence establishes that the 1st Plaintiff suffers from spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, severe developmental impairment, recurrent seizure disorder, scoliosis and lifelong dependency upon others for the ordinary activities of daily living. 4. The assessment of damages in a case of this nature is an exercise of considerable difficulty. No award of damages is capable of restoring the life which the 1st Plaintiff would otherwise have enjoyed. 5. The law nevertheless requires the Court to award fair and reasonable compensation for the injuries sustained and the consequences flowing therefrom. 6. These grounds set out the Court's reasons for the assessment of damages, including the treatment of expert evidence, compliance with case management directions, future care requirements, multiplier determination and aggravated damages.

judgments.title: GREAT EASTERN LIFE ASSURANCE (MALAYSIA) BERHAD v PERUSAHAAN OTOMOBIL NASIONAL SDN. BHD. & ors
judgments.catchwords: CIVIL PROCEDURE: Appeal — Consolidated appeals from Sessions Court — Appellate interference with findings of fact — Whether trial judge's findings plainly wrong or affected by insufficient judicial appreciation of evidence — Whether two judgments involving the same monetary sum but different causes of action were legally inconsistent — Whether appellate intervention warranted. INSURANCE: Insurance premiums — Group hospitalisation and surgical insurance policies — Recovery of alleged outstanding premiums — Payment by policyholder to insurance broker pursuant to established course of dealing — Whether payment to broker discharged policyholder's contractual payment obligations — Whether insurer's non-receipt of premiums established policyholder's indebtedness — Whether insurer proved outstanding premiums and claims excess. EVIDENCE: Burden of proof — Sections 101 and 106 of Evidence Act 1950 — Proof of liquidated debt — Invoices, debit notes and premium reconciliation — Incomplete documentary evidence — Whether insurer discharged burden of proving specific outstanding sums — Facts especially within knowledge of insurance broker — Whether broker's failure to provide satisfactory accounting justified adverse evidential conclusions. RESTITUTION: Unjust enrichment — Third-party proceedings against insurance broker — Premium monies received for specified purpose — Failure to account for or remit monies after authorised deductions — Whether independent restitutionary liability could arise notwithstanding dismissal of insurer's claim against policyholder — Whether monetary award sustainable on unjust enrichment principles. INDEMNITY: Third-party claim — Distinction between contingent indemnity and independent restitutionary cause of action — Whether dismissal of principal claim extinguished third-party claim — Whether restitutionary relief could be granted independently of primary contractual liability. Held: Both appeals dismissed. Sessions Court's dismissal of the insurer's claim against the policyholder affirmed. Monetary judgment against the insurance broker for RM598,521.05, together with interest and costs, affirmed on the independent grounds of restitution and unjust enrichment.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya v Azhar Bin Amid
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Law — Penal Code — ss. 385 & 34 — Extortion — Common intention — Accused police officer charged with putting victim in fear of injury/arrest to extort RM700 in common intention with four co-accused — Failure to prove a physical act of extortion or prior pre-arranged plan—Primary victim explicitly exonerated accused during cross-examination—Mere presence in vehicle insufficient to establish common intention—Whether prima facie case established Criminal Procedure—Appeal—Appeal against acquittal at close of prosecution case—Duty of appellate court—Standard of review —"Maximum evaluation" test—Audio-visual advantage of trial judge—Whether decision of learned magistrate in acquitting accused without calling for defence was plainly wrong—Criminal Procedure Code, s. 180(1) Evidence—Witnesses—Credibility—Material contradictions—Conflict between testimony of primary victim and accomplice witnesses regarding identity of physical perpetrator—Accomplice witnesses giving mutually destructive versions—Prosecution failing to conduct impeachment proceedings under ss. 145 & 155 of the Evidence Act 1950—Unimpeached evidence remaining part of the record—Prosecution unable to disown its own witnesses under s. 114(b)—Benefit of doubt to accused Evidence—Identification parade—Tainted procedure—Investigating officer actively managing identification parade and showing suspect's photograph to victim beforehand—Dock identification carrying little weight following corrupted parade—Failure to call identification parade manager and co-accused—Adverse inference—Evidence Act 1950, s. 114(g) Constitutional Law & Public Policy—Presumption of innocence—Accused wearing police uniform—Public interest and moral indignation—Rule of Law—Public policy cannot substitute for strict proof beyond reasonable doubt
judgments.judge: YA Dr John Lee Kien How @ Mohammad Johan Lee

judgments.title: MD ZAINI BIN YUSOP v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: CRIMINAL LAW: Road Transport Act 1987—s. 41(1)—Causing death by reckless or dangerous driving—Essential statutory ingredients—Charge sheet omitted mandatory environmental yardsticks ("having regard to all the circumstances, including the nature, condition, and size of the road, and the amount of traffic")—Charge sheet substituted the behavioural element "secara merbahaya" (in a dangerous manner) with the mechanical element "dalam keadaan merbahaya" (in a dangerous condition)—Whether the charge sheet is fundamentally defective—Whether the omission is curable under Criminal Procedure Code s. 422—Two-pronged test in Low Seng Wah v Public Prosecutor — Actual 3-tier misleading of defence, prosecution, and trial magistrate—Trial magistrate misdirected herself by treating statutory contextual metrics as negative burdens to be disproved by prosecution—Reversal of statutory burden of proof—Incurable failure of justice under Criminal Procedure Code s. 422—Mustafa Kamal Mohamed lwn. Public Prosecutor followed—Permissibility of substituted conviction under Road Transport Act 1987 s. 43(1)—Whether conviction can stand on a legally contaminated trial record CRIMINAL PROCEDURE: Trial—Change of Magistrate—Proceedings revived under Criminal Procedure Code. 254A—Application for trial de novo or resumption of key witnesses under Criminal Procedure Code s. 261(1)—Refusal by succeeding magistrate—Reliance on Recorded Video and Transcript (RVT) video playback as complete surrogate for observing live witness demeanor—Credibility and technical admissions of PUSPAKOM inspector and investigating officer fiercely contested—Whether mechanical exercise of judicial discretion under Criminal Procedure Code s. 261(1) prejudiced fact-finding process—Infringement of constitutional guarantee to fair trial under Federal Constitution art. 5(1) CRIMINAL LAW: Defences—Sudden emergency and agony of the moment—Reflex action—Heavy Isuzu commercial timber lorry laden with mangrove logs—Abrupt braking of preceding vehicle coupled with sudden, unexpected loss of braking response—Accused swerved right into opposing traffic lane to avoid rear-end collision—Objective fault test—Whether involuntary reflex action in sudden emergency negates criminal fault under Road Transport Act 1987 s. 41(1)—Cantona Lim Xiang Kim v. Public Prosecutor applied EVIDENCE: Burden and standard of proof—Reasonable doubt—Pre-existing mechanical brake failure—PUSPAKOM expert witness conceded pre-existing brake failure was a distinct technical possibility ("Boleh terjadi")—Absence of tire friction or skid marks at locus—Circumstantial evidence admitting of two competing inferences—Whether court bound to adopt exculpatory inference favorable to accused—Principles in Jayaraman & Ors v Public Prosecutor and Mat v Public Prosecutor applied—Alleged contradiction between first information report ("saya brek") and sworn court testimony ("kelajuan masih sama")—Reconciling layman's immediate physical effort with mechanical non-response of vehicle EVIDENCE: Witnesses—Non-production of material eyewitnesses—Passenger in deceased's vehicle—Adverse inference under Evidence Act 1950 s. 114(g)—Distinguishing deliberate suppression from failure to call corroborative witnesses—Principles in Munusamy v. Public Prosecutor and Abdullah Zawawi v. Public Prosecutor—Unexplained omission leaving unbridged gap in prosecution narrative CIVIL LAW: Remedies—Criminal acquittal on procedural defect and standard of proof—Effect on civil proceedings—Whether acquittal operates as res judicata or issue estoppel—Civil claims for dependency and negligence under Civil Law Act 1956 ss. 7 & 11 are determined on the balance of probabilities
judgments.judge: YA Dr John Lee Kien How @ Mohammad Johan Lee

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.catchwords: Civil Procedure — Appeal — Appeal from Sessions Court to High Court — Application to strike out Notice of Appeal — Dismissal of application to strike out pleadings — Whether appeal barred by section 28(1)(c) of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 — Whether refusal to strike out constituted a final determination of substantive rights — Applicability of the Federal Court decision in MT Ventures Sdn Bhd & Anor v QM Print Sdn Bhd and Another. Appeal — Whether preliminary questions of law rendered interlocutory order appealable — Whether separate corporate personality and alleged deficiencies in pleading conspiracy constituted independent legal bars to proceedings — Whether burden of defending action amounted to deprivation of substantive rights — Whether High Court possessed appellate jurisdiction — Notice of Appeal struck out. Company Law — Directors — Separate legal personality — Personal liability of company directors in negligence and conspiracy — Whether directorship alone sufficient to impose personal liability — Whether allegations of personal wrongdoing required determination at trial — Whether refusal to strike out claims against directors conclusively determined their substantive rights. Civil Procedure — Pleadings — Conspiracy — Alleged failure to plead material facts and particulars of conspiracy — Whether deficiencies in pleading justified striking out — Whether refusal to strike out defective pleadings constituted an appealable decision — Distinction between merits of striking-out application and competency of appeal.
